name: Apollo 17 science station
intro: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt set up the last Apollo science station in December 1972, about 190 meters west of Challenger. It measured heat, dust, gas and gravity, and it felt explosive charges the crew left on their drives. It worked until NASA ended support in 1977.

hotspots.title: The central station
hotspots.text: The station’s brain and radio. In September 1977 NASA stopped collecting its data and switched its experiments off, though its heat probes were still sending accurate readings.

video.caption: TV view from the rover of Harrison Schmitt setting up the science station.
video.credit: NASA (Apollo 17 television; ALSJ clip digitized by Peter Dayton)

hotspots.title: The gravimeter
hotspots.text: This instrument was meant to feel tiny ripples in gravity, but its weights were too light because of a factory mistake converting from Earth gravity to Moon gravity. Its sensor could never be balanced properly.

photo.alt: Instruments on the grey ground with a small antenna in front and a foil-covered gravimeter beyond.
photo.caption: The gravimeter stands beyond the seismic antenna, with Geophone Rock farther back.

hotspots.title: Listening for blasts
hotspots.text: Four geophones, small ground microphones, listened for eight explosive charges that the crew left up to 3.5 km away. The blasts revealed the rock layers down to about 3 km.

photo.alt: A small flag marks a spot on the grey ground, with the science station and rover in the distance.
photo.caption: A flag marks one geophone, with the station and rover behind.

hotspots.title: Heat probes
hotspots.text: Probes in two drilled holes measured heat seeping out of the Moon for 4 years and 10 months.

hotspots.title: The nuclear generator
hotspots.text: This finned can turned heat from plutonium into electricity, powering the station through the long lunar nights.

funFact: The eight explosive charges the crew left behind were set off by timers after they had flown away, so the station could feel the blasts.
whyLeft: It was built to keep working long after the last crew left, and it did, until NASA ended support for the Apollo stations in 1977.
repurpose: Its heat probes were still sending accurate readings when it was turned off, so it would be the best Apollo station to try waking up for a long-term temperature check.
